units.name: Case: an iron condor through expiry week
Case: hedging a portfolio before the Budget

terms.short: Buy a put, sell a lower put
terms.definition: Buying a put and selling a lower-strike put on the same expiry. It's a cheaper bearish bet than a put alone, and the profit is capped at the lower strike.
examples: Puts were rich after the fall, so we bought the 24,000–23,500 put spread instead of outright puts.
The strategist recommends the bear put spread on banks, since outright puts are pricey after the fall.
Risk likes the bear put spread for a bearish view, because the most it can lose is the premium paid.
terms.fill: Bearish, but put premiums were high, so she bought the 24,000 put and sold the 23,500 put: a ____.
wrong: Sell a put, buy a lower put
Sell a call, buy a higher call
Buy a call and a put at one strike

calcs.q: Buy the 24,000 put for 180 and sell the 23,500 put for 60. Maximum profit at expiry?
calcs.why: Spread width 500 minus the net cost of 120 = 380, earned if the Nifty ends at or below 23,500.

calcs.q: Same spread: buy the 24,000 put for 180, sell the 23,500 put for 60. Where does it break even at expiry?
calcs.why: Higher strike minus the net cost: 24,000 − 120 = 23,880.

terms.short: Sell a put, buy a lower put
terms.definition: Selling a put and buying a lower-strike put on the same expiry, for a net credit. It keeps the credit if the price stays above the higher strike, and the bought put caps the loss.
examples: Support at 23,800 looks solid, so we sold the 24,000–23,800 put spread for 60.
Risk caps the bull put spread book so one gap down can't wipe out a month's premium.
The client asked how she can earn if the market stays up or flat: sell the bull put spread below support.
terms.fill: Mildly bullish, he sold the 24,000 put and bought the 23,800 put, taking in 60 up front: a ____.
wrong: Buy a put, sell a lower put
Sell a call, buy a higher call
Sell a put with nothing bought

calcs.q: Sell the 24,000 put for 150 and buy the 23,800 put for 90. Maximum loss at expiry?
calcs.why: Width 200 minus the 60 collected = 140, lost if the Nifty ends at or below 23,800.

tf.s: A bull put spread keeps its whole credit if the underlying ends above the higher strike.
tf.why: Both puts expire worthless above the higher strike, so the credit is all profit.

terms.short: Sell a call, buy a higher call
terms.definition: Selling a call and buying a higher-strike call on the same expiry, for a net credit. It keeps the credit if the price stays below the lower strike, and the bought call caps the loss.
examples: The rally looks tired near 24,500, so we sold the 24,500–24,700 call spread.
The strategist prefers the bear call spread to a naked short call, because the loss is capped.
Risk checks the bear call spread's worst case, a rally through both strikes, before results.
terms.fill: Expecting the rally to stall below 24,500, she sold the 24,500 call and bought the 24,700 call for a net credit: a ____.
wrong: Buy a call, sell a higher call
Sell a put, buy a lower put
Sell a call on stock you own

calcs.q: Sell the 24,500 call for 110 and buy the 24,700 call for 50. Where does it break even at expiry?
calcs.why: Lower strike plus the net credit: 24,500 + 60 = 24,560.

terms.short: Buy one, sell more further out
terms.definition: Buying one option and selling more of a further out-of-the-money option of the same type and expiry, often for little or no cost. It makes the most if the price ends at the sold strike, but the extra short options leave open-ended risk on that side.
examples: The 1×2 call ratio costs almost nothing, but a big rally past 24,590 starts to hurt.
Risk flags every ratio spread because the extra short options can lose a lot in a big move.
The client asked why her ratio spread lost money when she was right on direction: the rally went too far.
terms.fill: He bought one 24,000 call and sold two 24,300 calls for almost nothing: a ____, with open-ended risk above.
wrong: Sell one, buy more further out
Buy one call, sell one higher call
Buy a call and a put at one strike

calcs.q: Buy one 24,000 call for 150 and sell two 24,300 calls for 70 each. Profit at expiry if the Nifty ends at 24,300?
calcs.why: The net cost is 150 − 140 = 10. At 24,300 the long call is worth 300 and the short calls expire worthless: 300 − 10 = 290.

tf.s: A 1×2 call ratio spread loses more and more as the price rises past its upper breakeven.
tf.why: Above the sold strike, two short calls lose faster than the one long call gains.

terms.short: Sell one, buy more further out
terms.definition: Selling one option and buying more of a further out-of-the-money option of the same type and expiry. It loses the most if the price ends at the bought strike, but gains without limit on a big move that way.
examples: We put on a call backspread before the policy meeting: small credit, and a lot of upside if the RBI surprises.
The strategist likes the put backspread before the election, since a crash would pay many times over.
Risk notes the backspread loses most if the market drifts to the bought strike and stops there.
terms.fill: Expecting a sharp rally, she sold one 24,000 call and bought two 24,300 calls: a call ____.
wrong: Buy one, sell more further out
Buy one call, sell one higher call
Sell a call and a put at one strike

calcs.q: Sell one 24,000 call for 150 and buy two 24,300 calls for 70 each. Profit or loss at expiry if the Nifty ends at 24,300?
calcs.why: The short 24,000 call costs 300 and the two 24,300 calls are worthless. The net credit of 10 cuts the loss to 290, the worst point.

terms.short: Buy an OTM call, sell an OTM put
terms.definition: Buying an out-of-the-money call and selling an out-of-the-money put on the same expiry, or the reverse, often for little net premium. It gains like long futures above the call strike and loses like it below the put strike. Its price is also used to measure skew.
examples: Puts are bid, so the 25-delta risk reversal is showing a steep skew.
The client asked why the analyst watches the risk reversal: it shows whether puts or calls cost more.
Risk asked the desk to explain its long risk reversal, since the sold put adds downside.
terms.fill: Bullish but unwilling to pay premium, she bought the 25,000 call and sold the 23,000 put for close to zero: a ____.
wrong: Own the stock, buy a put, sell a call
Buy a call and a put at one strike
Buy a call, sell a higher call

tf.s: A risk reversal with the call bought and the put sold loses money if the market falls far below the put strike.
tf.why: The sold put loses one for one below its strike, just like long futures.

terms.short: Own it, buy a put, sell a call
terms.definition: Owning the underlying, buying an out-of-the-money put and selling an out-of-the-money call to pay for it. Losses below the put strike and gains above the call strike are both cut off.
examples: The promoter collared the stake: bought 10% OTM puts and paid for them with 10% OTM calls.
The client asked whether the collar on her ESOP shares caps her gains too: yes, above the sold call.
Risk prefers the collar for the founder's stake, since it costs almost nothing up front.
terms.fill: To protect his shares cheaply, he bought a 5% out-of-the-money put and paid for it by selling a 5% out-of-the-money call: a ____.
wrong: Own it and sell a call only
Buy an OTM call, sell an OTM put
Buy a call and a put at one strike

calcs.q: You own a stock bought at 1,000, buy the 950 put for 15 and sell the 1,050 call for 12. Worst value of the holding at expiry, after the options?
calcs.why: The put floors the stock at 950, and the options cost a net 3, so the worst case is 947.

terms.short: Different strikes and expiries
terms.definition: Buying a longer-dated option and selling a nearer-dated one at a different strike. It mixes a calendar spread (different expiries) with a vertical spread (different strikes).
examples: We sold this week's 24,300 call against next month's 24,000 call, a diagonal that earns from the weekly's faster decay.
The strategist suggests the diagonal spread, selling the weekly against a longer-dated option.
Risk checks the diagonal spread each week, because the short leg expires first and must be rolled.
terms.fill: He bought next month's 24,000 call and sold this week's 24,300 call: a ____.
wrong: Same strike, different expiries
Same expiry, different strikes
Call and put at one strike and expiry

terms.short: Buy one, sell two, buy one, evenly spaced
terms.definition: Buying one option at a low strike, selling two at a middle strike and buying one at a high strike, all evenly spaced, of the same type and expiry. It costs little, makes the most if the price ends at the middle strike, and can lose only what was paid.
examples: With expiry on Tuesday and the Nifty pinned near 24,000, we bought the 23,800–24,000–24,200 call fly for 40.
The client asked how to bet that the Nifty ends near 24,000: buy the butterfly centred there.
Risk likes the butterfly because the most it can lose is the small premium paid.
terms.fill: For a cheap bet that the Nifty ends at 24,000, she bought the 23,800 call, sold two 24,000 calls and bought the 24,200 call, putting on the ____.
wrong: Buy one, sell one higher
Sell a call and a put at one strike
Buy one, sell two, with no top wing

calcs.q: Buy the 23,800 call for 290, sell two 24,000 calls for 160 each and buy the 24,200 call for 70. Maximum profit at expiry?
calcs.why: The net cost is 290 + 70 − 320 = 40. At 24,000 the 23,800 call is worth 200 and the rest expire worthless: 200 − 40 = 160.

terms.short: Short straddle with bought wings
terms.definition: Selling an at-the-money call and put at one strike and buying an out-of-the-money call and put as wings. It collects premium, makes the most if the price ends at the middle strike, and the wings cap the loss.
examples: Weekly IV is high, so we're selling the 24,000 iron fly with 300-point wings.
The strategist suggests the iron butterfly when IV is high and the index looks pinned.
Risk caps the loss on the iron butterfly at the wing width minus the credit.
terms.fill: She sold the 24,000 call and put and bought the 23,700 put and 24,300 call as protection, putting on the ____.
wrong: Short strangle with bought wings
Long straddle with sold wings
Call and put bought at one strike

calcs.q: Sell the 24,000 call for 150 and the 24,000 put for 140, buy the 24,300 call for 45 and the 23,700 put for 40. Maximum loss at expiry?
calcs.why: The net credit is 290 − 85 = 205. Past either wing the loss is the 300-point width minus the credit: 95.

terms.short: Butterfly with uneven wings
terms.definition: A butterfly with one wing further from the middle strike than the other. It can often be put on for a credit, leaving no risk on one side, while the far wing's side carries more risk than a normal butterfly.
examples: We skipped a strike on the upper wing, so the broken-wing fly went on for a small credit.
The strategist likes the broken-wing butterfly because it can be opened for a credit.
Risk asked where the broken-wing butterfly loses money: on a big move past the wider wing.
terms.fill: He bought the 23,800 call, sold two 24,000 calls and bought the 24,400 call instead of the 24,200, putting on the ____.
wrong: Butterfly with evenly spaced wings
Calendar spread at two strikes
Short straddle with no wings

tf.s: A call broken-wing butterfly opened for a net credit still makes money if the market falls below its lowest strike.
tf.why: Below the lowest strike every call expires worthless, so you keep the credit. The risk sits on the side of the wider wing.

terms.short: Gains from big moves or rising IV
terms.definition: A position that gains when the market moves more than expected or when implied volatility rises, such as owning straddles or strangles. It's long gamma and long vega, and it pays theta every day it waits.
examples: We're long vol into the election result; a quiet outcome will cost us a few days of decay.
The strategist recommends long volatility before the budget, since moves on the day are often bigger than priced.
Risk likes having some long volatility in the book to cushion a crash.
terms.fill: The desk bought straddles before the election result, so it went ____ into a possible shock.
wrong: Gains when the market stays calm
Gains when the price trends up
Gains when implied volatility falls

terms.short: Earns when moves are smaller than priced
terms.definition: A position that earns when the market moves less than implied volatility priced, such as selling straddles, strangles or iron condors. It collects theta but is short gamma and vega, so a sudden move or a jump in IV can wipe out months of gains.
examples: The fund's short-vol book made money for 11 months and gave most of it back in one gap down.
Risk limits short volatility in the book, because it loses most in a crash.
The client asked why her option-selling scheme lost a year's gains in one day: it was short volatility.
terms.fill: Selling strangles every week leaves the book ____: short gamma and short vega, so a sudden 3% gap hurts it.
wrong: Earns when moves are bigger than priced
Earns when implied volatility rises
Earns from a steady trend up

tf.s: A short volatility book usually shows small steady gains and rare large losses.
tf.why: It collects premium most days and gives much of it back in a sharp move. That's why sizing matters more than the win rate.

terms.short: Implied vol usually above realised
terms.definition: The usual gap by which implied volatility exceeds the volatility that later turns up. Option buyers pay it as insurance, and it's what option sellers earn on average in exchange for big losses in crashes.
examples: If implied keeps running 2 points over realised, selling vol pays, until the crash month.
The analyst says the volatility risk premium is why selling index options pays on average.
Risk warns that the volatility risk premium is pay for taking crash risk, not free money.
terms.fill: Index options usually price more movement than turns up, and that gap, the ____, is what option sellers are paid to bear crash risk.
wrong: Realised vol usually above implied
Extra return for holding small caps
Gap between futures and spot prices

tf.s: The volatility risk premium means selling index options makes money every month.
tf.why: It's an average. Sellers earn it in most months and lose heavily in some, such as March 2020.

terms.short: Trade implied vol against your forecast
terms.definition: Trading the gap between an option's implied volatility and the volatility you expect to be realised: buying options and hedging their delta when implied looks cheap, selling and hedging when it looks dear. The profit comes from volatility, not direction.
examples: Our forecast says 18% and the market prices 14%, so the vol arb desk is buying straddles and hedging daily.
Risk reviews the volatility arbitrage book's vol forecasts every week.
The client asked how a fund makes money from options without guessing direction: volatility arbitrage.
terms.fill: Buying options when implied vol looks cheap against your forecast and selling them when it looks dear, hedging delta each time, is ____.
wrong: Trade price direction with options
Lock in a price gap between exchanges
Buy a stock and sell its futures

terms.short: Index vol against its stocks' vol
terms.definition: Selling volatility on an index and buying volatility on its member stocks, or the reverse. It's a bet on correlation: when the stocks move apart, the stock options pay more than the index options cost.
examples: Correlation is high going into results season, so we're putting on dispersion: short Nifty vol, long vol on the top ten names.
Risk worries the dispersion trade loses if all the stocks crash together.
The strategist thinks the dispersion trade looks good when index vol is rich against single-stock vol.
terms.fill: The desk sold Nifty straddles and bought straddles on its biggest stocks, betting they'd move apart. The trade is called ____.
wrong: Buy the index, short its weakest stock
Spread one month's futures against the next
Sell options on one stock at two strikes

tf.s: A dispersion trade that is short index volatility and long stock volatility gains when the stocks become more correlated.
tf.why: It gains when correlation falls. Stocks moving apart make the stock options pay, while the index, where the moves cancel out, stays calm.

terms.short: P&L at expiry against price
terms.definition: A chart of a position's profit or loss at expiry against the underlying's price. It shows the breakevens, the maximum profit and the maximum loss at a glance.
examples: Draw the payoff before you trade it: I want to see where this loses money.
The client asked to see the payoff diagram before agreeing to the strategy.
Risk reads the payoff diagram for every new structure to find where it loses most.
terms.fill: Before placing the iron condor, she drew its ____: one line of profit and loss at expiry for every Nifty level from 23,000 to 25,000.
wrong: Chart of price against time
Chart of implied vol by strike
Chart of open interest by strike

terms.short: Expiry price with zero profit or loss
terms.definition: The underlying's price at expiry where a position neither makes nor loses money, once the premium paid or received is counted. A strategy can have one breakeven or two.
examples: The straddle's breakevens are 23,600 and 24,400; anything inside that and we lose.
The client asked how far the Nifty must rise for her call to pay off; the breakeven is the strike plus the premium.
Risk checks how far each position's breakeven is from today's price.
terms.fill: She bought the 24,000 call for 150, so her ____ at expiry is 24,150.
wrong: The most a position can lose
The strike of the option sold
Price at which an order is triggered

calcs.q: You buy the 1,000 put for 25. Where does it break even at expiry?
calcs.why: A long put breaks even at the strike minus the premium: 1,000 − 25 = 975.

terms.short: The most a position can lose
terms.definition: The most a position can lose, usually counted at expiry. It's the premium for a bought option or a debit spread, the width minus the credit for a credit spread, and unlimited for a naked short call.
examples: Max loss on the spread is ₹9,100 a lot, so we can run five lots inside the limit.
Risk sizes every option spread by its maximum loss, not its margin.
The client asked what her maximum loss is on the bought call: just the premium paid.
terms.fill: The risk desk sizes each spread by its ____: for this credit spread, the 200-point width minus the 60 collected, times the lot size.
wrong: The most a position can make
Premium paid to open a position
Margin blocked by the broker

calcs.q: You sell the 24,500–24,700 call spread for a 60 credit. The lot size is 65. Maximum loss per lot, in rupees?
calcs.why: Width 200 minus the 60 credit = 140 points, and 140 × 65 = ₹9,100.

terms.short: Premium paid to open a position
terms.definition: The premium you pay to open a position whose bought options cost more than its sold ones, as in a bull call or bear put spread. For such a spread, it's also the most you can lose.
examples: The put spread costs a 120 net debit, and that's all it can lose.
Risk likes spreads where the net debit is also the worst case.
The client asked why ₹6,000 left her account when she opened the spread: that's the net debit.
terms.fill: Buying the put for 180 and selling the lower put for 60 means paying a ____ of 120 to open the spread.
wrong: Premium received to open a position
The most a position can make
Margin paid on a short option

terms.short: Premium received to open a position
terms.definition: The premium you take in to open a position whose sold options are worth more than its bought ones, as in a bull put or bear call spread. It's the most such a position can make.
examples: We're short the condor for a 70 net credit.
The client asked why money came into her account when she opened the condor: the net credit.
Risk notes the net credit on the strangle is small next to what it can lose.
terms.fill: Selling the 24,000 put for 150 and buying the 23,800 put for 90, she receives a ____ of 60 into her account on day one.
wrong: Premium paid to open a position
The most a position can lose
Margin released after a trade

terms.short: Chance a position ends in profit
terms.definition: The chance a position makes money at expiry, usually estimated from implied volatility. Selling far out-of-the-money options gives a high chance of a small profit, and a much bigger loss when it fails.
examples: The strangle shows 85% to make money, but the 15% loses five times the 85% makes.
The client asked why a strategy with high probability of profit lost her money: the few losses were huge.
Risk never judges a trade by probability of profit alone; it looks at the size of the losses too.
terms.fill: Her short strangle had an 85% ____, yet one bad week wiped out ten good ones.
wrong: Average profit across all trades
Share of a portfolio in profit today
Chance an order gets filled

tf.s: A trade with a 90% probability of profit must have a positive expected value.
tf.why: The 10% of losing cases can be far bigger than the 90% of small wins. Expected value weighs both.

terms.short: Building a spread one leg at a time
terms.definition: Putting on a multi-leg position one leg at a time instead of all at once, hoping for better prices. The risk is that the market moves before the other legs are done.
examples: I legged into the condor: put side on the dip, call side on the bounce.
Risk warns that legging in can leave you with a naked option if the market moves before the second leg.
The client asked why her spread cost more than quoted: she was legging in and the price moved.
terms.fill: Instead of sending the iron condor as one order, he sold the put spread first and waited for a bounce to sell the call spread: ____.
wrong: Sending all the legs as one order
Closing a position before expiry
Moving a position to a later expiry

terms.short: Moving an option to a new strike or expiry
terms.definition: Closing an option position and opening the same kind of position at a later expiry or another strike, to give a trade more time or move it away from the price. It turns one trade into two, each with its own costs.
examples: The short call is in trouble; roll it up and out to next week's 24,800.
Risk watches traders who keep rolling options, because repeated rolls can hide a losing trade.
The client asked what rolling options means: closing this one and opening a similar one further out.
terms.fill: With the Nifty pressing on his short 24,500 call two days before expiry, he bought it back and sold next week's 24,800 call, ____.
wrong: Building a spread one leg at a time
Letting an option expire worthless
Exercising an option before expiry

terms.short: Lower margin for a hedged position
terms.definition: The lower margin an exchange charges for a hedged position, such as a spread, because SPAN looks at the worst loss of the whole position rather than each leg. A cheap bought wing can cut the margin on a short option by most of it.
examples: Add the far wing and the margin drops by about two thirds: that's the hedge benefit.
The client asked why adding a far OTM option cut her margin: that's the margin benefit of a hedge.
Risk counts on the margin benefit only while both legs are open.
terms.fill: Buying a cheap far wing against her short call cut the margin she needed from about ₹2 lakh to under ₹50,000, thanks to the ____.
wrong: Extra margin charged on expiry day
Interest earned on idle margin
Margin released after square-off

terms.short: Option traded on its expiry day
terms.definition: An option bought or sold on its expiry day, when almost no time value is left and gamma is at its highest, so small moves swing its price hard. Most expire worthless, and a few multiply.
examples: The 8-rupee expiry-day call went to 60 in an hour, then back to zero by the close.
Risk caps how much the desk can spend on any zero-day option, since most expire worthless.
The client asked why her zero-day option went from ₹10 to nothing by the close.
terms.fill: Bought at 10 a.m. on expiry day for 8 points, the Nifty call is a ____: by 3:30 it will either jump or go to zero.
wrong: Option with no strike price
Option that can't be exercised
Option listed on its first day

tf.s: On expiry day an out-of-the-money option's price reacts less to the underlying than it did a week earlier.
tf.why: Close to expiry, near-the-money options have their highest gamma, so a small move can multiply or wipe out the premium.

terms.short: Tax on an exercised option's value
terms.definition: Securities transaction tax charged when an in-the-money option is exercised at expiry, paid by the buyer on its intrinsic value. Since April 2026 it's 0.15%, the same rate a seller pays on premium, so letting an in-the-money option be exercised is no longer much dearer than selling it.
examples: Since April the exercise STT matches the sell-side rate, so the old expiry trap is mostly gone.
The client asked why tax was charged when her option was exercised: STT on exercise.
Risk used to close in-the-money options before expiry to avoid the high STT on exercise.
terms.fill: He let his in-the-money Nifty call be exercised at expiry and was charged 0.15% of its intrinsic value, the ____.
wrong: Tax on the premium when you sell
Fee the exchange charges per order
Margin blocked until settlement

calcs.q: An in-the-money call is exercised at expiry with an intrinsic value of 200 points. The lot size is 65. STT at 0.15%?
calcs.why: Intrinsic value is 200 × 65 = ₹13,000, and 0.15% of ₹13,000 is ₹19.50.

tf.s: Since April 2026, letting an in-the-money option be exercised costs far more STT than selling it before expiry.
tf.why: Both are now 0.15%: on intrinsic value when exercised, on premium when sold, and near expiry the two are close. The gap was big before October 2024, when selling was charged 0.0625%.

terms.short: Hedge sized by the portfolio's beta
terms.definition: Hedging a stock portfolio with index futures sized by its beta, so the market part of its moves is offset. The futures sold equal the beta times the portfolio's value; what's left is the stocks' own risk.
examples: Book beta is 1.15, so we're short ₹11.5 crore of Nifty futures against ₹10 crore of stock.
The client asked how a fund protects itself from a market fall without selling stocks: beta hedging with index futures.
Risk reviews the beta hedging each week, since the book's beta drifts as stocks move.
terms.fill: With a beta of 0.8 on her ₹5 crore portfolio, she sold ₹4 crore of Nifty futures, not ₹5 crore. That's ____.
wrong: Hedge sized by the portfolio's value
Hedge sized by the option's delta
Hedge with futures on a different month
terms.formula: Lots to sell = beta × portfolio value ÷ (futures price × lot size)

calcs.q: A ₹2 crore portfolio has a beta of 1.1. Nifty futures are at 25,000 and the lot size is 65. About how many lots do you sell to hedge it?
calcs.why: One lot is 25,000 × 65 = ₹16.25 lakh. 1.1 × ₹2 crore = ₹2.2 crore, and ₹2.2 crore ÷ ₹16.25 lakh ≈ 13.5, so about 14.

tf.s: A beta hedge protects a portfolio against a fall in any one of its stocks.
tf.why: It removes the market part of the moves. A stock falling on its own news still hurts.

terms.short: Hedge size per unit of exposure
terms.definition: How much of a hedging instrument you hold for each unit of exposure. A ratio of 1 hedges rupee for rupee; for a stock portfolio hedged with index futures it's usually the beta, and for an option it's the delta.
examples: Run the regression again: the hedge ratio has drifted from 1.1 to 0.95 since March.
The analyst estimates the hedge ratio from a year of daily returns.
Risk checks the hedge ratio before results season, when stocks stop tracking the index.
terms.fill: Before hedging the dollars due in June, the treasurer set the ____ at 1: one dollar sold forward for every dollar due.
wrong: Share of a portfolio held in cash
Margin as a share of position size
Gap between futures and spot prices

calcs.q: You'll hedge ₹6 crore of stocks with a beta of 1.25 using Nifty futures. What value of futures does the hedge ratio call for?
calcs.why: The hedge ratio is the beta, 1.25, so 1.25 × ₹6 crore = ₹7.5 crore of futures.

terms.short: Buy futures now for a later purchase
terms.definition: Buying futures now to lock in the price of something you'll buy later, such as a fund that expects new money next week and buys index futures until it can buy the stocks.
examples: Inflows land on Monday, so we've bought Nifty futures today and will swap them for stock as the cash arrives.
The PM's anticipatory hedge locked in today's price for money arriving next week.
Risk treats the anticipatory hedge as a real long position until the stock is bought.
terms.fill: Expecting ₹100 crore of new money next week, the fund bought Nifty futures today to lock in the market level, a classic ____.
wrong: Sell futures to protect stocks you own
Buy one month's futures, sell the next
Buy a put to cap a loss

terms.short: Hedge bigger than the exposure
terms.definition: Holding a hedge larger than the exposure it covers, so the extra part is a bet the other way. It often happens when a position shrinks and the hedge isn't cut to match.
examples: We sold half the stocks but not the futures, so we're over-hedged and now net short the market.
Risk flagged over-hedging after the fund sold stocks but kept its short futures.
The client asked why her hedged portfolio lost money in a rally: over-hedging made her net short.
terms.fill: After selling half the stocks but leaving all the short Nifty futures on, the fund was ____, and a rally would now cost it money.
wrong: Hedge smaller than the exposure
Hedge on a different month's futures
Hedge that expires before the exposure

tf.s: An over-hedged long portfolio makes money if the market falls.
tf.why: The short futures are bigger than the stocks, so a fall gains more on the futures than it loses on the stocks.

terms.short: Long one month's futures, short another
terms.definition: Buying one month's futures and selling another month's on the same underlying. It bets on the gap between them, not on the price, so exchanges usually charge it much less margin than an outright position.
examples: We're long the Feb–March roll: buy March, sell Feb, betting the gap widens.
Risk sees the futures calendar spread as low risk, since both legs move with the same index.
The analyst says the futures calendar spread widens when interest rates rise.
terms.fill: Expecting the roll cost to widen as funding got dearer, he bought March Nifty futures and sold February, putting on the ____.
wrong: Buy futures and the stocks in the index
Buy a call, sell a later call
Sell futures to protect a portfolio

calcs.q: February Nifty futures are at 25,100 and March at 25,260. You buy March and sell February. A week later February is at 25,050 and March at 25,240. Profit per unit?
calcs.why: Long March lost 20 and short February made 50: +30. The gap widened from 160 to 190.

terms.short: Long futures plus a bought put
terms.definition: Long futures plus a bought put at one strike. At expiry it pays like a bought call at that strike: the loss below the strike is capped, and the gain above it is open.
examples: Long futures into results with the 24,000 put underneath: a synthetic call, so the downside is known.
Risk treats the synthetic call like a bought call: the put caps the loss on the futures.
The strategist suggests the synthetic call for clients who already hold futures and fear a fall.
terms.fill: Long Nifty futures into results, he also bought the 24,000 put. With the loss capped below 24,000 and the upside open, his position is a ____.
wrong: Short futures plus a bought call
Long call plus a short put
Long futures plus a sold call

calcs.q: You're long Nifty futures at 24,100 and buy the 24,000 put for 150. Worst loss at expiry, per unit?
calcs.why: Below 24,000 the put offsets every point. You lose the 100 from 24,100 to 24,000 plus the 150 premium: 250.

terms.short: Short futures plus a bought call
terms.definition: Short futures plus a bought call at one strike. At expiry it pays like a bought put at that strike: the loss in a rally is capped above the strike, and the gain in a fall is open.
examples: Short futures before the policy with the 24,500 call on top, so a surprise cut can't run us over.
Risk treats the synthetic put like a bought put: the call caps the loss on the short futures.
The client asked why she bought a call while shorting futures: the pair is a synthetic put.
terms.fill: Short Nifty futures before the RBI decision, she bought the 24,500 call too. Her loss is capped above 24,500 and a fall still pays: a ____.
wrong: Long futures plus a bought put
Long put plus a short call
Short futures plus a sold put

calcs.q: You're short Nifty futures at 24,400 and buy the 24,500 call for 90. Worst loss at expiry, per unit?
calcs.why: Above 24,500 the call offsets every point. You lose the 100 from 24,400 to 24,500 plus the 90 premium: 190.

terms.short: Betting on the gap between put and call vols
terms.definition: A trade on the shape of the smile rather than the level of volatility: for example selling rich downside puts and buying cheaper upside calls, delta-hedged, when puts look too expensive against calls.
examples: Put skew is at a one-year high, so we're running a skew trade: sell the 25-delta puts, buy the 25-delta calls, delta-hedged.
The PM asked whether the loss was vol or skew. Level was flat; the skew trade lost because puts got even richer.
Risk flags that a short-put skew trade loses fast in a crash, exactly when skew steepens.
terms.fill: Downside puts looked far too rich against calls, so the desk sold puts, bought calls and hedged the delta: a ____.
wrong: Buying both puts and calls before an event
Selling the front month and buying the back month
Hedging delta with futures every hour

tf.s: A skew trade can lose money even when the overall level of implied volatility doesn't move.
tf.why: It is a bet on the difference between put and call vols, so a steeper skew hurts a short-skew position even with ATM vol unchanged.

terms.short: Betting on near vs far implied vol
terms.definition: A trade on the gap between implied volatility in near and far expiries, usually with calendar spreads: selling expensive near-month vol and buying cheaper far-month vol, or the reverse.
examples: Weekly vol is 4 points over monthly into the event, so we sell weeklies and buy monthlies: a term-structure trade.
After the event the curve flattened and the term-structure trade made back most of the premium.
She's long term structure in Bank Nifty: long the far month, short the near, betting the curve steepens back.
terms.fill: With near-month IV well above the far month before results, he sold the near expiry and bought the far: a ____.
wrong: A trade on put vol against call vol
Buying a bond and selling a longer bond
Selling options only on expiry day

terms.short: Cheap protection against a crash
terms.definition: Protection that pays off only in a rare, large fall, such as far out-of-the-money index puts or put spreads. It costs a little every month and is meant to pay many times its cost in a crash.
examples: We spend about 30 bps a year on a tail hedge: 10% out-of-the-money Nifty puts, rolled every month.
The tail hedge bled for two years and paid for both of them in one week in March.
The CIO wants a tail hedge before the election, but not one that costs more than a quarter of expected returns.
terms.fill: The fund buys far out-of-the-money index puts every month that only pay off in a crash: its ____.
wrong: Selling far out-of-the-money puts for income
A stop-loss placed just below support
Hedging only the last hour of a trading day

calcs.q: A ₹500 crore fund buys Nifty puts costing 0.3% of the fund each quarter. What does the tail hedge cost a year?
calcs.why: 0.3% a quarter is 1.2% a year: 1.2% of ₹500 crore = ₹6 crore.

terms.short: A swap paying realised vs agreed variance
terms.definition: An over-the-counter contract that pays the difference between the variance an index actually realises and a strike agreed at the start. It gives pure exposure to volatility, with no delta to hedge.
examples: The bank quoted a one-year variance swap on Nifty struck at 16 vol.
Short variance swaps earned steady carry until the crash, when realised vol went to 60.
We use variance swaps for vol exposure so we don't have to delta-hedge options every day.
terms.fill: Instead of buying options and hedging delta every day, the fund took clean exposure to realised volatility with a ____.
wrong: A swap of fixed for floating interest
A futures contract on India VIX
A trade that swaps puts for calls

tf.s: A long variance swap needs daily delta hedging.
tf.why: It pays on realised variance directly, which is why funds use it instead of a delta-hedged options book.

terms.short: Selling options as a steady, sized strategy
terms.definition: Selling options systematically, usually delta-hedged and sized to a risk budget, to collect the gap between implied and realised volatility. It earns small amounts most of the time and loses heavily in shocks, so sizing and tail hedges decide whether it survives.
examples: Our short-vol programme sells weekly Nifty strangles, hedges delta twice a day and caps vega at ₹20 lakh.
The short-vol programme made money 46 weeks out of 52, and gave back five months in the flash crash.
Risk wants every short-vol programme paired with a tail hedge.
terms.fill: The desk sells delta-hedged strangles every week, sized to a vega limit, to earn the volatility premium: a ____.
wrong: A plan to buy options before every event
Short-selling stocks with high volatility
A programme that shorts India VIX futures only

terms.short: Short put plus short call spread, no upside risk
terms.definition: Selling a put and a call spread at the same time, collecting more premium in total than the call spread is wide. That leaves no loss if the market rallies; the risk is all on the downside, like a short put.
examples: Premiums were rich, so she put on a jade lizard: short the 24,500 put, short the 25,500–25,700 call spread.
The jade lizard took in 260 against a 200-wide call spread, so a rally can't lose money.
Risk treats a jade lizard like a short put, since that's where all the loss is.
terms.fill: She sold a put and a call spread, taking in more premium than the call spread's width so a rally couldn't hurt: a ____.
wrong: Buying a put and selling a call spread
A long straddle with a short wing
Two calendar spreads at different strikes

calcs.q: A jade lizard: sell a put for 150, sell a 25,500 call for 140 and buy the 25,700 call for 30. How much can it lose if Nifty ends at 26,000?
calcs.why: Premium taken: 150 + 140 − 30 = 260. Above 25,700 the call spread loses its full width, 200, so you keep 260 − 200 = 60.

terms.short: Short a put, buy two lower puts
terms.definition: Selling one put and buying two lower-strike puts, often for close to zero cost. It loses a little if the market drifts down to the lower strikes and makes money if the market falls hard, so it is a cheap bet on a crash.
examples: Instead of buying puts outright, he did a short put ladder: sold the 24,000, bought the 23,500 and 23,000 for almost nothing.
The short put ladder's worst case is a slow grind to 23,500; it pays in a crash.
The desk likes short put ladders before events where a big fall is possible but not the base case.
terms.fill: He sold the 24,000 put and bought the 23,500 and 23,000 puts for close to zero, losing only if Nifty drifted to the lower strikes: a ____.
wrong: Buying one put and selling two lower puts
Selling puts at every strike down the chain
Rolling a short put down each week

terms.short: Trading ahead of index funds' forced flows
terms.definition: Positioning ahead of the buying and selling that index funds and ETFs must do when an index changes its weights or members, usually at the close on the effective date. Traders buy expected inclusions and weight increases, and sell what index funds must sell.
examples: Passive funds have to buy ₹2,000 crore of the stock at the close on rebalance day, so the index rebalancing trade is crowded.
We sized the index rebalancing trade at 20% of expected passive flow, because the close can't absorb more.
The index rebalancing trade reversed the day after the change, as it often does.
terms.fill: Knowing passive funds must buy the new members at the close on the effective date, the desk bought them a week before: an ____.
wrong: Rebalancing your own portfolio once a quarter
Selling an index future to hedge a stock book
Buying all fifty stocks in an index at once

terms.short: A stock joining an index, and the buying after
terms.definition: When a stock is added to an index such as the Nifty 50 or an MSCI index. Every fund that tracks the index must buy it, so the price often rises between the announcement and the effective date, and may fall back after.
examples: MSCI inclusion could bring about $300 million of passive buying into the stock.
The stock ran 12% from the index inclusion announcement to the effective date, then gave back half.
Analysts track free float and size to predict the next index inclusion.
terms.fill: The stock was named a new Nifty 50 member, so tracker funds had to buy it: an ____.
wrong: A stock leaving an index after falling
Listing a company's shares on the exchange
A fund adding a stock it already owns

calcs.q: Passive funds tracking an index hold ₹40,000 crore. A newly included stock gets a 0.5% weight. How much must they buy?
calcs.why: 0.5% of ₹40,000 crore = ₹200 crore, usually bought at the close on the effective date.

terms.short: Prices keep moving the way results surprised
terms.definition: The tendency of a stock to keep drifting for weeks in the direction of an earnings surprise, rather than adjusting all at once. Known as PEAD, it is one of the oldest documented anomalies, and quants trade it by buying big positive surprises and selling big negative ones.
examples: The PEAD signal buys the top decile of earnings surprises and holds them for 60 days.
The beat was huge but the stock only rose 3% on the day; post-earnings drift says there's more to come.
Post-earnings drift is weaker in large caps now that more funds trade it.
terms.fill: After a big earnings beat, the stock kept rising for weeks instead of jumping once: ____.
wrong: The price fall just before results come out
A drop in implied volatility after results
Brokers revising targets after results

terms.short: A straddle bought or sold into earnings
terms.definition: A straddle put on just before a company's results, to trade the size of the move rather than its direction. Buyers win if the stock moves more than the straddle's price implies; sellers win from the IV crush if it moves less.
examples: The results straddle prices a 6% move; it's moved more than 6% on only two of the last eight results.
We sold the results straddle and bought wings, since IV crush after the call usually beats the move.
Buying the results straddle only pays if the surprise is bigger than the market expects.
terms.fill: The day before earnings, she sold the at-the-money call and put to bet the move would be smaller than priced: a ____.
wrong: Buying the stock and a put before results
A calendar spread across two results dates
Selling futures before the results call

calcs.q: A ₹1,500 stock has a results straddle priced at ₹90. What move does it imply?
calcs.why: The straddle's price is roughly the expected move: 90 ÷ 1,500 = 6%.

terms.short: Buying shares to tender into a buyback
terms.definition: Buying a stock below the buyback price to tender it in a tender-offer buyback. The profit depends on the acceptance ratio, the share of tendered shares the company actually takes, since the rest must be sold back in the market. Since October 2024 the whole buyback payout is taxed as dividend income in India, which has cut into the trade.
examples: The buyback is at ₹1,800 against ₹1,650 in the market, but buyback arbitrage only works if the acceptance ratio is decent.
Small shareholders get a reserved quota, so buyback arbitrage is popular with retail.
Our buyback arbitrage made ₹40 a share after the unaccepted shares fell back to ₹1,620.
terms.fill: The company offered ₹1,800 a share in a tender buyback while the stock traded at ₹1,650, so traders bought to tender: ____.
wrong: The company buying its own shares in the open market
Short-selling a stock after a buyback ends
Buying shares in an IPO to sell on listing

calcs.q: Buy 100 shares at ₹1,650 to tender at ₹1,800. The acceptance ratio is 40%; the rest are sold at ₹1,620. Profit?
calcs.why: 40 shares gain ₹150 each = ₹6,000; 60 shares lose ₹30 each = −₹1,800. Net ₹4,200.

terms.short: Trading the discount when a big holder sells
terms.definition: Trading around a large sale by a promoter or private equity holder, usually placed at a discount to the market price through a block deal. Traders buy in the block at the discount and sell later, or short ahead if they expect more supply.
examples: The PE fund is selling 4% through a block deal at a 5% discount; the block-deal trade is to get an allocation and sell over a week.
Desks short ahead of a block-deal trade when a lock-in expiry is coming up.
The block-deal trade worked: the stock was back above the deal price two days later.
terms.fill: A private equity holder sold 5% at a 6% discount; she bought in the deal and sold over the next week: a ____.
wrong: Buying a block of options at once
Selling shares when a stock hits its upper circuit
A promoter pledging shares for a loan

terms.short: Trading futures against the index basket
terms.definition: Buying or selling the stocks in an index against the index future when the future is too far from fair value, and unwinding at expiry when the future settles to the index. On expiry it means trading the basket at the close to match the settlement price.
examples: The future is 40 points rich against fair value, so index arbitrage sells futures and buys the basket.
Index arbitrage desks unwind into the close on expiry, which is why the last half-hour is so busy.
Index arbitrage keeps Nifty futures within a few points of fair value most of the time.
terms.fill: The Nifty future traded 40 points above fair value, so the desk sold it and bought the fifty stocks, unwinding at expiry: ____.
wrong: Buying the index on one exchange and selling on another
Trading Nifty options against Bank Nifty options
Holding the index for the long term

terms.short: Trading the futures basis around dividends
terms.definition: A trade on how futures price an upcoming dividend. A stock future should sit below the cash price plus carry by the expected dividend; if the market misjudges the dividend, traders take cash against futures and profit when the dividend is announced or paid.
examples: The futures price a ₹20 dividend, but we expect ₹35, so the dividend basis trade is to buy futures and sell cash.
A surprise special dividend blew up everyone short the dividend basis trade.
The dividend basis trade is small per share, so the desk runs it across many stocks at once.
terms.fill: Futures priced a ₹20 dividend while the desk expected ₹35, so it bought futures against cash: a ____.
wrong: Buying high-dividend stocks for income
Selling a stock the day before it goes ex-dividend
Rolling futures to the next month for the yield

terms.short: Trading a break of the first minutes' range
terms.definition: An intraday style that marks the high and low of the first 15 or 30 minutes and trades in the direction the price breaks out of that range, with a stop on the other side.
examples: Nifty's first 15 minutes ran 24,880 to 24,960; the opening range breakout buys above 24,960 with a stop at 24,880.
Opening range breakouts fail a lot on quiet days, so he only trades them after a gap.
The backtest says the opening range breakout makes money on trend days and gives it back on range days.
terms.fill: He marked the high and low of the first 15 minutes and bought when the price broke above the high: an ____.
wrong: Buying in the pre-open session
Trading the gap between yesterday's close and today's open
Selling options at 9:20 every morning

calcs.q: The opening range is 24,880 to 24,960. You buy the breakout at 24,965 with a stop at the range low, and target twice the risk. Target?
calcs.why: Risk is 24,965 − 24,880 = 85 points; twice that is 170, so the target is 24,965 + 170 = 25,135.

terms.short: Fading moves away from the day's VWAP
terms.definition: An intraday mean-reversion style that sells when the price stretches well above the day's VWAP and buys when it stretches well below, expecting it to drift back. It works on range days and loses on trend days.
examples: The stock is 1.5% above VWAP with no news, so the VWAP reversion setup is to short it back toward VWAP.
VWAP reversion got run over today; it was a trend day and price never came back.
Institutional desks benchmark to VWAP, which is one reason VWAP reversion works at all.
terms.fill: On a quiet day, she sold whenever the price got 1% above the day's average traded price, betting it would come back: ____.
wrong: Buying stocks that trade above their VWAP
An execution algo that tracks VWAP
Resetting VWAP at noon each day

terms.short: Holding trades for days to a few weeks
terms.definition: Trading moves that last from a couple of days to a few weeks, between intraday and investing. Swing traders hold overnight, so they carry gap risk, and use daily charts for entries and stops.
examples: He's a swing trader: buys pullbacks in strong stocks and holds three to ten days.
Swing trading means overnight gaps; size so a 5% gap against you doesn't hurt.
Most of her swing trading is in cash, not futures, so she doesn't pay rollover.
terms.fill: He buys pullbacks in trending stocks and usually holds them for three days to two weeks: ____.
wrong: Trading only in the first hour
Holding stocks for many years
Switching between long and short every minute

terms.short: Selling options on their last day for fast decay
terms.definition: Selling options on the day they expire, when time decay is fastest and premiums shrink to nothing by the close. It wins small most days and can lose big when the index moves sharply, which is why gamma risk on expiry day draws so much regulatory attention in India.
examples: Expiry-day option selling looks like free money until a 300-point move takes out a month of premium.
SEBI's expiry-day margin was aimed partly at expiry-day option selling.
She does expiry-day option selling with defined risk: short straddle, long wings.
terms.fill: Every weekly expiry he sold at-the-money options in the morning to collect the fastest decay of the month: ____.
wrong: Buying options on expiry day for a gamma blast
Selling futures before they expire
Rolling options to the next expiry

terms.short: Price returning to close an opening gap
terms.definition: When a stock or index that opened with a gap trades back to the previous close. Gap-fill traders fade gaps that have no strong news behind them; gaps on big news often don't fill.
examples: Nifty gapped up 120 points on global cues; the gap fill trade shorts for a move back to yesterday's close.
That gap won't fill: it's on results, not on SGX noise.
Three of the last four gap-downs saw a gap fill by lunch.
terms.fill: Nifty opened 120 points higher on no real news and was back at yesterday's close by noon: a ____.
wrong: The pre-open price matching the close
Filling a limit order at the gap price
A gap between bid and ask

terms.short: Betting long yields rise vs short yields
terms.definition: A trade that profits when the yield curve gets steeper: the gap between long-term and short-term yields widens. It is usually done by buying short bonds and selling long bonds, with sizes matched by PV01 so that a parallel move does nothing.
examples: If the RBI cuts and the fiscal deficit stays wide, a 2s10s steepener should work.
We put on the steepener PV01-neutral: long ₹100 crore of the 2-year against short the matching risk in the 10-year.
The steepener lost as long yields fell faster than short ones.
terms.fill: Expecting rate cuts but a wider deficit, the trader bought 2-year bonds and sold 10-year bonds, matched by PV01: a ____.
wrong: Buying bonds of every maturity
A trade that profits when the curve flattens
Raising the repo rate in steps

terms.short: Betting the yield curve flattens
terms.definition: A trade that profits when the gap between long-term and short-term yields narrows, usually by selling short bonds and buying long bonds in PV01-matched sizes. It often works when the central bank is hiking.
examples: With the RBI hiking, the 2s10s flattener has made 30 basis points.
He put on a flattener: short the 3-year, long the 10-year, PV01-neutral.
Flatteners worked all year as short yields rose with the policy rate.
terms.fill: With the RBI hiking, she sold 2-year bonds and bought 10-year bonds in matched risk, betting the gap would narrow: a ____.
wrong: Selling bonds of every maturity
A bond that pays the same coupon every year
Cutting the CRR to add liquidity

calcs.q: The 2-year yields 6.6% and the 10-year 7.1%. A month later they're 6.9% and 7.2%. How much did the 2s10s spread move, and did a flattener win?
calcs.why: The spread went from 50 bps to 30 bps, narrowing 20 bps, which is what a flattener needs.

terms.short: Gain as a bond ages down the yield curve
terms.definition: The return a bond earns as it gets closer to maturity and is valued at the lower yield of a shorter bond, on an upward-sloping curve with no change in rates. Rates desks add carry and roll-down to judge what a position earns if nothing happens.
examples: The 5-year sits on the steepest part of the curve, so it has the best roll-down.
Carry plus roll-down on the position is about 40 basis points a year if the curve doesn't move.
Roll-down disappears when the curve is flat.
terms.fill: With the curve unchanged, the 5-year bond became a 4-year bond priced at a lower yield, and gained in price: its ____.
wrong: Rolling a futures contract to the next month
A fall in coupon after a rate cut
Selling bonds as they get close to maturity

terms.short: Trading one government bond against another
terms.definition: Buying a government bond that looks cheap against the curve and selling a similar one that looks rich, in matched risk, betting the gap closes. Typical trades are a bond against its neighbours, a new issue against an older one, or a G-sec against an SDL.
examples: The 2033 looks 6 basis points cheap to the fitted curve, so the G-sec relative value trade buys it against the 2032 and 2034.
SDL spreads over G-secs are wide this auction; that's a relative value trade.
G-sec relative value books run small risk and need repo to fund the long side.
terms.fill: The 2033 bond looked 6 bps cheap to its neighbours, so the desk bought it and sold the 2032 and 2034 in matched risk: a ____ trade.
wrong: Comparing a stock's PE with its sector
Buying any government bond yielding over 7%
The RBI buying bonds in an OMO

terms.short: Trading views on economies across markets
terms.definition: A style that takes positions across currencies, rates, equity indices and commodities based on views about growth, inflation, central banks and politics. Macro funds size by risk and move between markets as the story changes.
examples: The global macro fund is short the yen and long Indian bonds on the rate-cut story.
A global macro PM wants to know the RBI's reaction function, not one company's earnings.
Global macro had a great year as rates moved more than they had in a decade.
terms.fill: The fund trades currencies, bond futures and equity indices around the world on views about inflation and central banks: ____.
wrong: Investing only in large companies worldwide
Buying an index fund that covers every country
A strategy that trades macro data releases intraday only
